proposal.description:
Every proxy you run today was designed for a world where routing decisions live in paths, hosts, and headers. AI traffic broke that assumption. Which model? Which provider? Is this an MCP call or a chat completion? The answers are buried in JSON bodies - invisible to nginx, awkward in Envoy, and increasingly the difference between a demo and a production system.
This talk introduces Praxis, an open-source proxy framework built for AI infrastructure. We'll look at what makes AI workloads genuinely different - body-based routing, credential isolation, streaming-first traffic, token-denominated cost, and agent protocols like MCP - and why bolting these onto existing proxies keeps failing. Then we'll dig into why Praxis is written in Rust: zero unsafe code and Rustls in the most exposed component of your stack, predictable latency with no GC jitter, and the ability to stand on Cloudflare's battle-tested Pingora rather than reimplementing HTTP.
Crucially, Praxis is a framework for building proxies, not just a proxy. Everything is a filter - routing, rate limiting, guardrails, model selection - and your custom filters use the same traits as the built-ins, compiling straight into the binary. The same primitives compose into an AI gateway, an ingress, an egress proxy, or a mesh sidecar. Whatever your use case, you can assemble it from config in minutes - and when no filter fits, write your own and make the proxy truly yours.

speakers.bio: Alex Snaps is a senior principal software engineer at Red Hat, where he works on several open source projects related, directly or indirectly, to the CNCF-hosted Kuadrant project — most recently shifted focus on AI networking and gateway infrastructure. Passionate about distributed systems, programming languages, and performance-related topics, he's currently deep in Rust, tackling systems-level problems from streaming parsers to WebAssembly targets. He has had the good fortune of combining his passion with open source development for nearly 20 years — having written his first lines of code at the age of 8, and never stopped since, more than 40 years later.

proposal.summary: Praxis is an open-source Rust proxy framework built for AI traffic, enabling body-based routing, credential isolation, streaming, token-cost controls, and MCP support. Unlike traditional proxies, it uses composable filters for routing, guardrails, rate limiting, and custom logic, letting teams build AI gateways, ingress, egress, or sidecars quickly.
proposal.title: The Praxis proxy or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love AI workloads

track.name: Cloud Native, Data & Infrastructure
track.description: Kubernetes, platform engineering, vector DBs, model serving, and GPU orchestration.

proposal.description:
Java 28 will soon introduce, as a preview feature, value classes (JEP 401), a new kind of class that renounces its identity to get better performance.

In this presentation, we will explain what value classes are, how the Java spec was re-interpreted to conjure their existence, how they interact with existing code and what optimizations they enable both on the stack and the heap.

To make it concrete, we'll explore these ideas through the simulation and rendering of a black hole: calculating the trajectories of thousands of light rays through curved spacetime means manipulating huge numbers of vectors, rays, coordinates, and intermediate values.

Finally, we will look ahead at the experimental "!" syntax for null-restricted types, its optimization potential, and the limitations of the current design.

Join us to discover value classes and the current state of Project Valhalla.

speakers.bio:
Passionate about software development since getting my first programmable calculator, I have built a solid experience as a tech lead and architect in designing embedded combat systems.
An advocate of clean code, "developer joy" and well-thought-out architectures, I enjoy working on design topics as well as front-end or back-end development.
I recently founded a "JUG-like" meetup in southern France called "Toulon Dev"

Tenured associate professor at Université Gustave Eiffel (Paris) and longtime OpenJDK member researching runtime environments (Java VM, .NET). He has contributed to major Java features including invokedynamic (JSR 292), Lambda (JSR 335), and the Jigsaw module system (JSR 376), and currently works on OpenJDK's Amber (records, pattern matching) and Valhalla (value types) projects. He's also the main contributor to the ASM bytecode library.
A frequent conference speaker (Devoxx France, FOSDEM), he regularly presents on modern Java features like virtual threads, structured concurrency, and value types.

proposal.summary: This talk introduces Java’s Project Valhalla value types through a black hole simulation, showing how they improve immutability, memory efficiency, and performance for heavy numerical workloads. It also explores experimental non-nullable `!` syntax, optimization potential, current limitations, and practical benchmarks.
proposal.title: Escaping Java's Allocation Gravity with Value Classes

track.name: Java Language & Platform
track.description: Project Loom, Leyden, Valhalla, Panama, and the ever evolving JVM.

proposal.description:
After years of rounding off a square peg to fit into Java's mainline, JEP 401's value objects are coming to OpenJDK in its first preview. It is a single keyword change, you don't even need to recompile your libraries, yet there's so much happening. What you can learn here:

  • What value objects are, why and how you want to use them
  • What value objects do for the Java Virtual Machine, and therefore your code
  • Where Is OpenJDK going with this: "healing the rift" between objects and primitives

There will be some project history, concerning peak Valhalla prototype performance, and how all the dangerous bits were smoothed off to make it usable. There will be some JVM engineering details on implementation and a peek at some wild and crazy ideas for the future, hoping to be a few thesis papers in the coming months. The audience should come away with an understanding that, whilst we don't quite yet have `List<int>`, there is a path to get there, which you will see with JEP 401.

In the meantime, JEP 401 Value Objects, holds plenty of subtle language features and interactions with the JVM to help your code be better from a safety and clarity point of view and also some performance wins along the way, with the promise of more to come...

speakers.bio:
Hands on Java Virtual Machine engineering for over 25 years, first with the JRockit VM and then Hotspot JVM. Involved in Project Valhalla over 10 years now, I might have filed an almost 3000 commit PR to integrate the first really big step in getting Valhalla into OpenJDK. On the side I manage Oracle's Java Platform Group engineering site in Stockholm Sweden.

"Kiwede" - New Zealander living in Sweden

proposal.summary: JEP 401 Value Objects arrives in OpenJDK preview, enabling a new Java type model with minimal code changes. The talk explains what value objects are, JVM benefits, Valhalla history, implementation details, and the path toward bridging objects and primitives, including future support like `List<int>`.
proposal.title: Why it takes 3000 commits to bring Valhalla's value objects to the JDK

track.name: Java Language & Platform
track.description: Project Loom, Leyden, Valhalla, Panama, and the ever evolving JVM.

proposal.description:
Maven is more than 20 years old, and it's last major version (Maven 3) was released in 2010. Since then Maven got several great updates, but the Maven team also realized that Maven can't evolve further without huge changes which have the capability to break the whole ecosystem if done wrong. Now - after years of intensive planning and coding - the release of Maven 4 is closer than ever before!

In this talk I'll speak about the motivation and challenges the team had while developing Maven 4 and of course about its new features and improvements.

speakers.bio: Matthias loves Java, Jakarta EE / Microprofile, testing and documentation. He is a Maven committer and maintainer of the JUnit extension library "JUnit Pioneer".

proposal.summary: This talk explores Maven 4’s long-awaited development, the challenges of evolving a mature ecosystem without breaking compatibility, and the motivations behind its redesign. It also highlights key new features and improvements in the upcoming major release.
proposal.title: All you need to know about Maven 4!

track.name: Development Practices
track.description: All about Getting Stuff Done right. Methodologies, better practices, etc.

proposal.description:
So you got "promoted" to lead a team / project / whatever. What now? Do you have what it takes? It certainly seems that your hierarchy thinks so. But oftentimes things are not so black and white. Being a great plumber doesn't automatically make you a great leader of plumbers, so you need to adapt and adjust your ways of working by dropping old habits and picking up new ones. Then you start getting worried by the fact that you won't be able to have as much impact as before, since you're not coding as much as you used to in the past (and that's what you're good at, right?).

What if leadership can amplify your technical impact instead? In this talk, I’ll share how I evolved from individual contributor to a mix of Solution Architect, Tech Lead and classical Engineering Manager at CERN - keeping my hands in the code while scaling my influence through the team that I work with. I'll be sharing best practices and adjustment techniques for you to use when faced with the difficult transition process into technical leadership. And lastly, we'll be talking about how to stay relevant even if you're not spending countless hours honing your coding skills anymore.

speakers.bio:
Dr. Cristian Schuszter holds a PhD in Systems Engineering with a focus on distributed fault-tolerant software architectures and machine-learning based failure prediction. In his day-to-day, he is somewhere between a Data and Full-stack Software Engineer, with a wide range of tech & job exposure both in academia and industry.

For the past 8 years he's been working with various teams in CERN (the European Organization for Nuclear Research). Currently he's focusing on the architectural directions of the CERN business computing group, with an emphasis on enterprise Java systems and UI.

proposal.summary: This talk explores the transition from individual contributor to technical leader, showing how leadership can amplify impact rather than reduce it. Drawing on experience at CERN, it shares practical techniques for adapting, staying relevant, and maintaining technical influence while leading teams.
proposal.title: The Quantum Tech Lead: Hands-On and Abstract at the Same Time

track.name: People, Practices & Career
track.description: Leading teams, engineering culture, and career resilience.

proposal.description:
Most agent frameworks ask a language model to decide what to do next. That works, until it doesn't — and when it doesn't, you're left with a non-reproducible trace and no way to explain what happened. Embabel takes the opposite approach.

Created by Rod Johnson — who calls it the most important project since founding Spring — Embabel is a JVM-native agent framework built on Spring AI and Spring Boot. Its core is Goal-Oriented Action Planning (GOAP), an algorithm borrowed from game AI: you declare goals, annotate actions with @Action and @AchievesGoal, and a deterministic, non-LLM planner chains them by pre- and post-conditions to reach the goal. The plan is code-generated, inspectable before it runs, and explainable afterwards. If Spring AI and LangChain4j are the Servlet API of GenAI, Embabel is Spring MVC.

Full presentation details pending.

speakers.bio: Rod Johnson is a developer, author, entrepreneur and advisor. He is the creator of the Spring Framework and Embabel agent framework.

proposal.summary: Embabel is a JVM-native agent framework built on Spring AI and Spring Boot that replaces LLM-driven decision-making with deterministic Goal-Oriented Action Planning (GOAP). Developers declare goals and actions; a code-generated planner chains them by conditions, producing inspectable, reproducible, and explainable execution traces.
proposal.title: Embabel Agent v1.5

track.name: Agentic Engineering & Tooling
track.description: Multi-agent systems, tool-use, evals, and shipping AI beyond the demo.

proposal.description:
For the last 20-30 years, the software industry has been learning — sometimes the hard way — how to build better software. Practices like TDD, refactoring, pair programming, simple design, collective code ownership, continuous integration, and coding standards didn't appear by magic. They came from pain, failed projects, and the brilliant minds behind XP — Kent Beck, Ward Cunningham, and Ron Jeffries — who asked: "can we do this better?"

And now? Now we have AI. And suddenly, some developers are asking: "do we still need all that?"

In this session, we'll look at 7 XP practices that are genuinely at risk in an AI-assisted world — not because they're wrong, but because AI makes it tempting to skip them. We'll see what happens when teams do skip them (spoiler: it's not pretty 😅), and more importantly, how these practices don't just survive the AI era — they become *more critical than ever*.

AI amplifies everything. Good habits and bad ones. If your team has no tests, no shared standards, no feedback loop — AI will help you build the mess of your life, faster than ever before.

AI is the best stress test XP practices have ever had. Spoiler: they pass 😉

speakers.bio:
Nacho is a software engineer from Barcelona, fan of eXtreme Programming (XP) practices who has been working with Java and other web technologies before the Y2K. He had experience in different roles in the IT world ('guy-for-everything', developer, team lead, project manager and CTO) working in companies in many sectors: energy, e-commerce, startups (some unicorn) technology consultancy and application performance management. Now working as a Principal Software Engineer at Dynatrace developing software for monitoring applications and in 2022 became Java Champion.
Always concerned with questions like "how does it work?" and "how can we make it better?", Nacho loves to share his knowledge with others and learn from them. As a natural progression to this attitude, he founded the Barcelona Java Users Group and co-founded the Barcelona Developers Conference (DevBcn).
When he is not thinking about the next interesting thing to do for the community, he enjoys spending time with his family, playing sports or improving his TDD and other XP skills.

proposal.summary: AI can tempt teams to skip core XP practices like TDD, refactoring, pair programming, and CI. This session shows why these habits are at risk in AI-assisted development, what breaks when they’re ignored, and why they matter even more as AI accelerates both good and bad engineering.
proposal.title: Is AI killing XP practices? (Or are we letting it?)

proposal.description:
Project Amber has introduced a series of Java language features that together
enable a new programming style: data oriented programming. At its core is
compositional pattern matching, which allows values to be deconstructed
naturally and safely.

Where does Project Amber go from here? This talk explores the next wave of
language features under development. These experiments extend pattern matching
in several directions, including user-defined deconstruction for ordinary
interfaces and classes, nested constant patterns for more compact and expressive
matching, an exhaustive pattern-matching statement, safer primitive value
conversions within pattern matching, and a compact notation for deconstructing
and constructing record instances — a process we call reconstruction.

Along the way, I’ll present some of the experimental designs we’re exploring,
discussing both the opportunities they create and the language design challenges
they raise.

speakers.bio:
I work in the Java Platform Group at Oracle designing the Java programming language and virtual machine. I am also a member of the Programming Languages Research Group at Oracle Labs. I am based in Cambridge, UK.
My mission is to keep Java as a leading language and platform for developers around the world. Given my background as a researcher, I am especially keen to find, adapt and transfer ideas and techniques from the research community and get them into the hands of Java programmers. I spend much of my time working on Java’s industry-leading specifications.

I joined Oracle in March 2014. Previously I was a senior researcher at Microsoft Research Cambridge from March 2004 until February 2014. Before that I was a University Lecturer at the University of Cambridge Computer Laboratory and a Fellow, College Lecturer and Director of Studies at St John’s College, Cambridge. I studied for my PhD at the University of Cambridge, and for my BSc at Imperial College, London.

proposal.summary: Project Amber is advancing Java’s data-oriented programming with new pattern-matching features: user-defined deconstruction, nested constant patterns, exhaustive matching, safer primitive conversions, and compact record reconstruction. The talk explores experimental designs, their benefits, and the language design challenges they introduce.
proposal.title: What’s happening with Project Amber?

track.name: Java Language & Platform
track.description: Project Loom, Leyden, Valhalla, Panama, and the ever evolving JVM.

proposal.description:
In our job, technical debt is probably the most frustrating, draining and tenacious thing we have to fight against. Of course, there are best practices: refactor, aim for simplicity with KISS, avoid over-engineering with YAGNI in order to keep this debt as low as possible. And yet, we never really manage to get rid of it. Worse, it keeps piling up even when we apply those principles, as if it were inevitable.

But what if those very best practices sometimes made the problem worse instead of solving it? Technical debt may be only the visible part of something deeper: accidental design debt. A far more complex problem that leads to spaghetti software and microservices that are really just a distributed monolith, and that we often create ourselves without even realizing it.

In this talk, we will explore the mechanisms of design debt and its impact on our architecture, our processes, our organization, and even our business. Through concrete examples, we will see how to detect it, assess how deep it goes, and act before it becomes entrenched for good.

speakers.bio: Julien is a CTO and hands-on technical coach with 15 years+ of experience, specializing in Domain-Driven Design (#DDD). His expertise lies in helping organizations build systems that deliver high business value. Julien focuses on aligning organizational structure, architecture and software practices with business objectives. As a member of the OWASP foundation, he actively promotes application security best practices. An international speaker, Julien enjoys sharing his knowledge with others.

Tech coach at Shodo, specializing in AI assisted development, Domain Driven Design and Flow. He helps organizations improve their practices and systems, from architecture and code to org structure and process.

proposal.summary: The talk argues that technical debt is only the surface of deeper accidental design debt, which can worsen despite best practices like refactoring, KISS, and YAGNI. It explores how design debt forms, affects architecture and business, and how to detect, assess, and prevent it.
proposal.title: You thought technical debt was bad? Meet design debt!

proposal.description:
What happens when your architecture doesn't just fail a performance test, but triggers a national regulatory investigation? In this session, we go inside a critical system failure at a major bank that led to a formal report to BaFin and a complete rethink of our data strategy.
Dealing with 11TB of data on Oracle Exadata taught us that at a certain scale—specifically, the 10-billion-record mark—standard indexing strategies and read-side duplicate checks don't just slow down; they collapse. We will reverse-engineer this incident by walking through the five critical architectural milestones:
  1. First Aid: Immediate application-layer mitigation steps to halt cascading timeouts.
  2. The Refactoring Oversight: How a missing 10-day query window check, removed years prior, silently waited to trigger an 11TB full scan.
  3. The Cache Bottleneck: The high-stakes "do nothing" war room decision to wait for the Exadata Smart Flash Cache to warm up and recover.
  4. The Structural Flip: Moving 10kB of complex analytic queries from read-side deduplication to a write-side integrity layer.
  5. The Exit Strategy: Designing and planning a zero-loss dual-write ingestion architecture to migrate 10 billion records to Cloud PostgreSQL without CDC.
Walk away with an unvarnished, practical blueprint for navigating the compliance-performance paradox, handling database cold starts, and executing a zero-loss cloud modernization strategy under heavy pressure.

speakers.bio:
Martin Ladecký is an enterprise architect and systems engineer dedicated to building resilient, high-scale data infrastructure and promoting clean engineering practices. Operating within heavily regulated financial environments, he specialises in optimising core Java workloads, container stability, and complex multi-terabyte database ecosystems.
As an active contributor to the European open-source and tech community, Martin balances his corporate work at scale with meaningful "Tech for Good" initiatives. He organises the Czech Java User Group and contributes to Česko.Digital to help NPOs change lives through technology.
When he isn’t diving into thread dumps or troubleshooting connection pools, you can usually find him exploring local running trails or enjoying a great espresso.

proposal.summary: A major bank incident triggered a BaFin investigation after an 11TB Oracle Exadata system failed at 10 billion records. This session examines emergency mitigation, a missed query-window check, cache warming, shifting deduplication to writes, and designing zero-loss dual-write migration to Cloud PostgreSQL.
proposal.title: 10 Billion Records vs. The Regulator: An Architectural Post-Mortem of an 11TB Exadata Failure

track.name: Architecture & Modernization

proposal.description:
In the 1970s, model trains were a popular hobby. Thanks to low production costs, anyone could afford a small HO gauge layout. The system was simple: a train, a motor, 12V DC in the track, and off you go!

Fifty years later, we took our trains out of the attic with a big idea in mind: to convert them to digital. With some Seeed Studio, Bluetooth, and TinyGo, we managed to get a functional railway network, were we can manage speed, direction, and lights of each train individually.

This talk speaks about hardware and software architecture for embedded systems, in a retrospective format about all our successes (and mistakes) during the conception of this project. Everything is open-source, so don't hesitate to use it, fork it, and enhance it!

speakers.bio:
French developer working at Zenika. I spent 5 years working for a sovereign cloud provider, deploying OpenStack at scale and extending it with Golang-written software. Passionate about everything related to IT, especially if it's new to me!

Also, I like trains, so I put some RP2040/nRF52840 in my HO models to control them. Have a look at https://github.com/trainberry if you're interested!

Oh, and, as my name can prefigure it, I'm French... Sorry if I make some english mistakes.

I'm a developper in a sovereign cloud infrastructure. My day-to-day life is filled with Openstack, Golang, DevOps automations and network problems !

I'm passionate about IT, photography and lots of different drawing or sculpting technics. To sum up : I love learning as much as I can !

proposal.summary: A retro model train hobby project was modernized with Seeed Studio hardware, Bluetooth, and TinyGo to create a digital railway network with individual train control for speed, direction, and lights. The talk covers embedded hardware/software architecture, lessons learned, and open-source implementation.
proposal.title: My old trains have a second life, with TinyGo!

track.name: Mind the Geek
track.description: Developer candy: stuff we want to know about but dont (generally) at work, Robotics, biological computing, cybernetics, AI, new toys, tomorrows world

proposal.description:
I was about ten years into my Java career when I had spoken at enough conferences, and befriended enough speakers, that my sense for the hype cycle had been sharpened by the collective skepticism of the speaker jet-set. That was two decades ago. We've all heard the latest hype about what AI agents can do well. Less hyped is what can go wrong: non-determinism, DRY violations, hallucinated APIs, token cost, unreviewable code, and code reviews that start to improve the code, only to keep going until the code is actually broken.

This talk makes the case that it's the time-honed boring things about Java that keep the agents honest. Successful agentic development maximizes agent strengths — speed, breadth, fearless exploration, tolerance for boilerplate — while backstopping their weaknesses: non-determinism, dependency sprawl, inconsistent error handling, and code that works but nobody wants to maintain.

Here are the 10 boring reasons:
1. Type system
2. Testing ecosystem
3. Backwards compatibility culture
4. Deep static analysis
5. Build system maturity and dependency management
6. Code formatting and style enforcement
7. Virtual threads and structured concurrency
8. Observability stack
9. JVM performance tuning
10. Breadth of deployment options

For each, I'll show the specific agentic failure mode it addresses. I'll close with a practical checklist for making your Java development process agent-safe, and tie it up with the message that to move forward, you have to go back.

speakers.bio:
Ed Burns is currently Principal Architect on the Java Tooling and Experiences team at Microsoft. In this role, Ed will help make Azure the best place for Enterprise Java. Prior to joining Microsoft, Ed was a Principal Member of the Technical Staff At Oracle. While there, Ed was the specification lead or co-lead for JavaServer Faces, the standard Web Application Framework for Java EE, and for Servlet, the standard HTTP API for Java EE. Ed continued in these roles from his work at Sun Microsystems, Inc. In these roles, Ed lead a team of web experts from across the industry in developing JavaServer Faces and Servlet Technology through the Java Community Process and in open source. His areas of professional interests include web application frameworks, AJAX, reducing complexity, test driven development, requirements gathering, and computer supported collaborative work. Before working on JavaServer Faces, Ed worked on a wide variety of client and server side web technologies since 1994, including NCSA Mosaic, Mozilla, the Sun Java Plugin, Jakarta Tomcat, the Cosmo Create HTML authoring tool, and the web transport layer in the Irix operating system from Silicon Graphics.
Ed has published four books with McGraw-Hill: JavaServerFaces: The Complete Reference (2006), Secrets of the Rockstar Programmers: Riding the IT crest (2008) JavaServer Faces 2.0: The Complete Reference (2010) and Hudson Continuous Integration In Practice (2013). To learn more about his books or projects, you can visit his website at <http://ridingthecrest.com/> or Amazon Author Page.
Ed has a Bachelor of Computer Science degree from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. While at UIUC, Ed took a minor in Germanic Studies and worked for IBM in the co-op program, where he first acquired a fondness for computer history by working on System 370 Office Software.
Ed is a frequent keynote speaker at international industry conferences, having presented many times at Oracle's JavaOneSM conference, given keynote addresses at Javaland, the JAX conference in Mainz, the W-JAX conference in Munich, Germany and the Globalcode Developer's Conference in São Paulo, Brazil, and the JSFDays conference in Vienna Austria. In addition to keynotes, Ed has given technical sessions at numerous international Java conferences including Javapolis, Jazoon, JAX-India, TheServerSide.com Java Symposium, No Fluff Just Stuff, the Ajax Experience, JAOO, and others, and also has spoken at many Java User Group meetings. A complete list of Ed's conference speaking experience is available at <http://purl.oclc.org/NET/edburns/speaking-engagements/> Further information and blogs may be found at <http://purl.oclc.org/NET/edburns/>.

proposal.summary: The talk argues that Java’s “boring” strengths—types, tests, static analysis, mature builds, formatting, observability, and more—help control AI agents’ risks like hallucinations, non-determinism, and unmaintainable code. It maps 10 Java features to agent failure modes and ends with a practical agent-safe checklist.
proposal.title: 10 boring reasons why Java is the best ecosystem for agentic development

track.name: Agentic Engineering & Tooling
track.description: Multi-agent systems, tool-use, evals, and shipping AI beyond the demo.

proposal.description:
Java's big projects are shaping its present and future. Over recent years, Amber and Leyden, Panama and Loom have greatly improved the
language, APIs, and runtime. But they're not done yet! And neither are Valhalla and Babylon - in fact they're just getting started.

Time to take a closer look at how...

  • Project Valhalla mends the rift in Java's type system
  • Project Leyden improves Java's startup and warmup time
  • Project Babylon extends the reach of Java to foreign programming models and hardware
  • Project Panama cuts through the isthmus separating Java from native code
  • Project Amber makes the language more expressive and ready for today's and tomorrow's problems
  • Project Loom further improves efficient, structured concurrency
  • Project Detroit allows simple interop with Python and JavaScript

After this talk, you will know what to expect from Java in the next few years and surely there's no better way to end a great Devoxx!

speakers.bio: Nicolai (aka nipafx) is a Java enthusiast focused on language features, core APIs, and runtime evolution with a passion for learning and sharing. He does that mostly at conferences and in his biweekly Inside Java Newscast, but also occasionally in podcasts, live streams, articles, and books - more on all that on nipafx.dev. He's a Java Developer Advocate at Oracle and otherwise best known for his haircut.

proposal.summary: This talk explores Java’s evolution and future through major projects: Valhalla’s unified type system, Leyden’s faster startup, Babylon’s foreign models and hardware support, Panama’s native interoperability, Amber’s expressive language features, Loom’s structured concurrency, and Detroit’s Python/JavaScript integration. Attendees will gain a roadmap of Java’s coming years.
proposal.title: Java Next - From Valhalla to Leyden, from Babylon to Panama, from Amber to Detroit

track.name: Java Language & Platform
track.description: Project Loom, Leyden, Valhalla, Panama, and the ever evolving JVM.

proposal.description:
Stuck in a legacy system that needs modernizing? Feel like the best course of action is to throw it in a dumpster, light it on fire and rewrite everything from scratch - maybe even in a different language?

Hold that thought. While it may be tempting to start a rewrite, rewrites of complicated systems rarely succeed for multiple reasons. Chief among them is time and the fact that not everything can stop and wait for the rewrite, but another important contributor is the second system effect, which usually causes rewrites to be over-engineered and bloated in comparison to what they replace

In this talk, I'll share my experiences with the Strangler Fig pattern, a better approach where the original system is gradually replaced by breaking out or rewriting parts into separate systems. I'll also talk about combining this with Domain Driven Design and how to use the new design to execute an Inverse Conway Manoeuvre to ensure you're working with Conway's law and not against it.

speakers.bio: Raniz is a programmer, architect, speaker and coach at factor10. He is a problem solver who keeps track of the bigger picture. He is prestigeless, likes to get into new domains, and loves sharing knowledge and ideas. Raniz has worked with system- and software architecture at several companies since 2010 and has been with factor10 since 2021. When not working he's into beer brewing, sourdough bread, 3D printing and triathlons.

proposal.summary: The talk argues against full rewrites of legacy systems, citing risk and the second system effect. It promotes the Strangler Fig pattern for gradual replacement, combined with Domain-Driven Design and the Inverse Conway Manoeuvre to align system architecture with team structure.
proposal.title: Strangling the dragon: modernizing legacy systems with the Strangler Fig pattern

track.name: Architecture & Modernization
track.description: Designing for agentic workflows, event-driven systems, and legacy transformation.

proposal.description:
Agentic AI is something everyone wants to use or sell. We wanted an overview of the work and active agents and therefore we created an orchestration tool. Using the Agent, Skills and Spec files from default locations so its interchangeable with other tools. And it really started to change the way we worked on software projects.

As a Java software Engineer it could be seen as a automation of tasks, as an Scrum Master/Product Owner a way to coordinate and for the business analyst a way to store functional requirements. We've used Embabel Agent as the fundamental layer. On top of that we've created a visual representation so we can have a website open in our office which shows which agent is active, what it's doing and what's the next task.

For Software Development teams this will be the biggest change, developers are more reviewing and delivering feedback to the AI while business analysts had a field day of delivering the requirements for the spec files which were reviewed by an AI agent before they could be assigned to an AI-agent. The product owner is in control of the queue where sprints are no longer weeks but days.

I want to share how we created this orchestrator and explain on which impact each technical step had on the way-of-work in our team. It wasn't just about creating an application anymore, everything had impact on how we work.

speakers.bio: CTO and Software Architect with over 10 years of hands-on java development experience.
